problem: A fintech runs a double-entry ledger service backing wallet-to-wallet transfers. It currently uses a single primary Postgres instance in us-east-1 with synchronous standbys. Regulators now require the service to remain writable from both the US and the EU even during a full regional outage, and EU customer balances must be physically stored in-region (data residency). You must recommend the data architecture and consistency model for the next two years. Competing constraints: (1) every transfer must preserve the invariant that debits equal credits with no double-spend, globally; (2) p99 transfer-confirmation latency must stay under 400ms for in-region users; (3) the system must accept writes in each region during cross-region network partitions (target survivability: 30+ min isolation); (4) EU personal balance data must not be replicated to US storage; (5) finance reconciliation needs a globally consistent end-of-day snapshot; (6) the team is 6 engineers with no prior multi-region operational experience and a 9-month deadline. Recommend the replication topology, conflict/ordering strategy, and how transfers that span a US and an EU wallet are settled, and justify the tradeoffs you accept.

You own the recommendation platform at a mid-size e-commerce company. Models are trained in nightly Spark batch jobs over a data lake, but served online with sub-50ms feature lookups from a key-value store. The team keeps shipping models that look strong offline (high AUC on held-out data) but underperform or degrade in production within days. You must design the feature platform and evaluation methodology to fix this. Competing constraints: (1) online and offline features must be computed from logically identical definitions to avoid train/serve skew, yet some features (e.g., 'items viewed in last 5 minutes') are only cheaply computable online; (2) offline backfills must reproduce the exact feature values a model would have seen at a past timestamp (point-in-time correctness), across years of history; (3) feature freshness for some signals must be under 1 minute online; (4) storage and compute budget is fixed and already 70% consumed; (5) data scientists must be able to add new features without platform-team involvement; (6) GDPR deletion requests must propagate to both training data and online stores within 30 days. Recommend the architecture, the offline/online consistency mechanism, and the evaluation protocol that would have caught the degradations earlier.

A SaaS analytics product stores all tenant event data in one 12TB MySQL database that is now hitting write IOPS and lock-contention limits during peak ingestion. You must recommend and design a migration to a sharded architecture, executed with no maintenance window, while the system continues ingesting ~80k events/sec and serving dashboard queries. Competing constraints: (1) absolutely zero downtime and no dropped or duplicated events during the cutover; (2) some dashboard queries aggregate across tenants (cross-shard fan-out) and must keep sub-2s latency; (3) tenant sizes are extremely skewed — the largest tenant alone is 18% of total volume; (4) the migration must be reversible at any point if data drift is detected; (5) the existing app has thousands of raw SQL queries assuming a single database, and the app team can only afford limited query rewrites this quarter; (6) the new design must support adding shards later without another full migration. Recommend the sharding key strategy, the dual-write/backfill/cutover mechanism, how you handle the skewed mega-tenant and cross-shard queries, and how you verify correctness before and after cutover.

Your team runs a stateless API tier (containers behind a load balancer) plus a shared Redis cache and a Postgres backend, serving a consumer app with spiky, partly-predictable traffic: a 10x surge within 60 seconds when push notifications go out. Recent surges caused cascading failures — latency spiked, autoscaling lagged, the cache stampeded on cold keys, and the database connection pool saturated, taking the whole service down for 20 minutes. You must recommend an end-to-end scaling and resilience strategy. Competing constraints: (1) the service must absorb a 10x spike in under 60 seconds without falling over; (2) cloud cost must not balloon — sustained over-provisioning for the baseline is financially unacceptable; (3) cold-start time for new container instances is ~45 seconds; (4) Postgres can sustain only a fixed number of connections and is hard to scale vertically on short notice; (5) the cache layer must not stampede or serve dangerously stale data for write-sensitive endpoints; (6) graceful degradation is allowed (some features may shed load) but core read paths must stay available. Recommend the scaling triggers, capacity-provisioning approach, cache strategy, backpressure/load-shedding mechanism, and the database-protection design, and justify how they interact under the surge.

A mid-size B2C streaming-fitness app (480k paying subscribers, $14.99/mo) has flat net revenue and rising voluntary churn (3.1% monthly, up from 2.4% a year ago). Growth has asked you to recommend a single Q3 retention strategy from three candidates: (a) an annual-plan push with a 30%-off prepay offer, (b) a personalized 'pause instead of cancel' flow at the cancel screen, or (c) a content-velocity bet doubling new-class output for the next two quarters. You must pick one and justify it. Constraints: the annual discount hits cash-positive but compresses ARPU and front-loads refund liability; pause flows historically recover 40% of would-be cancellers but those users show 60% lower 6-month LTV; content production needs 9 weeks lead time and the data linking 'more content' to retention is correlational; the board wants net-revenue-retention above 100% by year-end; CAC has risen 22% so replacing churned users is costlier than last year; and engineering can only fully resource one of the three this quarter. Recommend which strategy to pursue and how to measure whether it worked.

A regional e-commerce furniture retailer ships from one 220k-sq-ft DC outside Columbus and is missing its 2-day-delivery promise on 18% of orders, concentrated in the Southeast and Texas. Leadership wants you to recommend whether to (a) open a second DC near Atlanta, (b) shift to a 3PL partner for Southeast fulfillment, or (c) re-slot the existing DC and renegotiate carrier zones without adding a node. You must choose and defend it. Constraints: a second DC costs ~$6.2M to stand up plus ~$3M/yr opex and takes 11 months to operational; the 3PL quote is variable-cost but 14% higher per unit at current volume and caps SKU breadth at 70% of the catalog; bulky-furniture freight is dominated by linehaul, not last-mile, so zone math differs from parcel; demand in the South is growing 25% YoY but from a smaller base; inventory split across two nodes raises safety-stock carrying cost; and the CFO wants any capital project to clear a 3-year payback. Recommend the option and the decision criteria.

A horizontal project-management SaaS (11k accounts, mostly SMB, seat-based at $12/seat/mo) is considering moving to usage-based pricing tied to 'active projects' to capture value from a few very large accounts that currently underpay relative to consumption. You must recommend whether to migrate, and if so, the migration design. Constraints: the top 8% of accounts drive 55% of infrastructure cost but only 30% of revenue under seat pricing; sales reps are comped on seat expansion and would resist a model that decouples revenue from seats; existing customers were sold annual contracts with seat-based terms that don't expire for up to 11 months; competitors are mostly still seat-based, so usage pricing is a differentiation risk in deals; finance wants revenue predictability for an upcoming raise; and early surveys show SMB customers fear 'unpredictable bills.' Recommend migrate / don't migrate / hybrid, the grandfathering and rollout sequence, and how you'd know within two quarters whether it's working.

A contract manufacturer of injection-molded parts (annual revenue $90M, EBITDA margin 12%) can invest $8M in either (a) two automated molding cells that cut direct labor on its highest-volume line by 35%, (b) a flexible cell that runs short-run custom jobs the company currently turns away, or (c) splitting the capital across debt paydown and a smaller automation pilot. You must recommend the allocation. Constraints: the high-volume line serves one customer at 38% of revenue whose contract renews in 19 months with no guarantee; the custom-job market is higher-margin (28% vs 14%) but lumpy and would require hiring scarce process engineers; the firm carries $22M floating-rate debt and rates have risen 250bps; the automation vendor quotes 14-month lead times and historical installs ran 20% over budget and schedule; labor is hard to rehire if cut and later needed; and the owner wants to preserve optionality for a possible sale in 3-4 years. Recommend the capital allocation and the assumptions it hinges on.
